tool.excerpt: The 2026 Bangladesh garment workers protests are a series of labour demonstrations by workers in the ready-made garment industry of Bangladesh, demanding an increase in the sector's minimum monthly wage from ৳12,500 to ৳30,000. Protests began in August 2026 and escalated in late October and early November 2026 in the industrial areas of Ashulia and Gazipur and in the capital, Dhaka. On 1 November 2026, the government announced the formation of a six-member Minimum Wage Board including factory owners, though protests continued after the announcement due to not meeting demands. == Background == Bangladesh's garment industry is the second-largest in the world, after China, and contributes about 10 percent of the country's gross domestic product. According to the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA), the industry has around 4,000 registered factories employing more than four million workers, an estimated 65 percent of whom are women. The sector's previous minimum wage of ৳8,000 was in place from 2018 and, according to the Fair Labor Association, had fallen below the World Bank poverty line for a two- to three-person household by 2022. The association also found that garment workers' wages had barely increased since 2019 despite high inflation. The current minimum of ৳12,500 was declared by the Minimum Wage Board in November 2023. The decision was followed by protests in Gazipur, and the Clean Clothes Campaign described the new rate as a "poverty wage". In April 2026 an amendment to the Bangladesh Labour Act reduced the minimum wage review cycle for the sector from five years to three. The Global Living Wage Coalition, using the Anker methodology, estimated the 2025 monthly living wage at ৳30,459 for Dhaka City and ৳25,166 for the satellite cities and districts surrounding Dhaka, where most of the country's garment industry is located. The Dhaka City estimate is based on a family of four with 1.58 full-time workers and a monthly cost of a basic but decent living of ৳48,022. == Protests == === August–October 2026 === In August 2026, garment workers in several parts of the country held protests demanding a minimum wage of around ৳30,000, c

The unrest, which began on Saturday, has intensified despite the government’s move to form a six-member wage board to review pay in Bangladesh’s garment sector, the world’s second-largest apparel exporter after China.
“It is crucial that brands act immediately and speak out in support of workers’ demands,” said Anne Bienias, from the Clean Clothes Campaign industry advocacy group.

The protests, which continued for the third day on Monday, come amid a prolonged economic slowdown, and just ahead of former prime minister Sheikh Hasina's proclaimed return to Bangladesh from exile in India.

As workers take to the streets amid rising inflation and stagnant wages, the government has accused Sheikh Hasina 's Awami League and "several people from across the border" of instigating the violence.
It was under Hasina that the ready-made garment industry, the backbone of Bangladesh's economy, grew massively.
The sector employs around four million workers, accounts for 80% of Bangladesh's export earnings and contributes about 10% of its GDP, according to data cited by Reuters.
However, the ready-made garment sector is now facing major disruption, with hundreds of factories shutting down over the weekend and nearly a million workers affected.
The demand comes amid a prolonged economic slowdown in Bangladesh .
The slowdown has also affected workers in the garment sector.

A Daily Star report published on October 22 noted that many garment workers were having to put in 16-hour shifts to earn Tk 19,000 to Tk 20,000 a month, barely enough to cover their families' expenses.

Following an emergency meeting with cabinet ministers late on Sunday, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman directed authorities to protect workers' interests while ensuring uninterrupted production in the garment sector.
That is why the Prime Minister has instructed everyone to be vigilant so that production in the garment sector is not disrupted and instability is not created," he told BBC Bangla.

The allegations went further on Monday, when Tarique's political assistant, Rashed Khan, accused Jamaat-e-Islami and the National Citizen Party (NCP) of instigating the protests, while claiming that Awami League and Chhatra League activists had joined demonstrations posing as garment workers.

In any case, for Bangladesh, the immediate challenge is twofold: restoring production in an industry that is critical to its export economy, while addressing the wage and working conditions that have brought its workforce onto the streets.
The violent protests, demanding higher wages, have brought large parts of its vital manufacturing sector to a standstill.
advertisement ❮ ❯ Read Full Story The World Bank has projected a GDP growth of just 3.4% in FY2025–26 for Bangladesh , the slowest pace of growth since the Covid year of 2020.
Several experts have suggested that Bangladesh's economy went downhill after Hasina was forced out on August 5, 2024.
Although some factories reopened on Monday, protests continued across Dhaka and other major garment hubs.
The violence intensified the following day in Dhaka's Mirpur, where workers blocked the Mirpur-10 intersection and clashed with police.
Protesters hurled bricks and stones at security personnel, who responded with tear gas, water cannons and baton charges, Prothom Alo and United News of Bangladesh reported.
In Gazipur, protesters torched a police box in Konabari , a garment-waste warehouse and a pickup van in Kaliakair.
In neighbouring Savar and Ashulia, factory premises were vandalised and a security booth at a garment factory in Hemayetpur was set on fire.
The Daily Star reported that police dispersed workers attempting to take to the streets in Mirpur, while Prothom Alo reported a fresh blockade of the Dhaka-Tangail Highway in Gazipur.
Ten platoons of the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) were deployed in the district.
The unrest has severely disrupted garment production.
A heavy police force and Border Guard Bangladesh have been deployed to restore order in the industrial areas.
At the heart of the protests is a demand for higher wages.
But meeting the demand for higher wages will be easier said than done.

tool.title: 2026 Bangladesh garment workers protests
tool.excerpt: The 2026 Bangladesh garment workers protests are a series of labour demonstrations by workers in the ready-made garment industry of Bangladesh, demanding an increase in the sector's minimum monthly wage from ৳12,500 to ৳30,000. Protests began in August 2026 and escalated in late October and early November 2026 in the industrial areas of Ashulia and Gazipur and in the capital, Dhaka. On 1 November 2026, the government announced the formation of a six-member Minimum Wage Board including factory owners, though protests continued after the announcement due to not meeting demands. == Background == Bangladesh's garment industry is the second-largest in the world, after China, and contributes about 10 percent of the country's gross domestic product. According to the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA), the industry has around 4,000 registered factories employing more than four million workers, an estimated 65 percent of whom are women. The sector's previous minimum wage of ৳8,000 was in place from 2018 and, according to the Fair Labor Association, had fallen below the World Bank poverty line for a two- to three-person household by 2022. The association also found that garment workers' wages had barely increased since 2019 despite high inflation. The current minimum of ৳12,500 was declared by the Minimum Wage Board in November 2023. The decision was followed by protests in Gazipur, and the Clean Clothes Campaign described the new rate as a "poverty wage". In April 2026 an amendment to the Bangladesh Labour Act reduced the minimum wage review cycle for the sector from five years to three. The Global Living Wage Coalition, using the Anker methodology, estimated the 2025 monthly living wage at ৳30,459 for Dhaka City and ৳25,166 for the satellite cities and districts surrounding Dhaka, where most of the country's garment industry is located. tool.title: Labor history of the United States
tool.excerpt: In June, he passed the National Industrial Recovery Act, which gave workers the right to organize into unions. Though it contained other provisions, like minimum wage and maximum hours, its most significant passage was, "Employees shall have the right to organize and bargain collectively through representative of their own choosing, and shall be free from the interference, restraint, or coercion of employers." This portion, which was known as Section 7(a), was symbolic to workers in the United States because it stripped employers of their rights to either coerce them or refuse to bargain with them. While no power of enforcement was written into the law, it "recognized the rights of the industrial working class in the United States". For example, the now United Mine Workers of America were able to reignite the coal labor movement in Kentucky and West Virginia with Section 7(a) and eliminated compulsory residence in company towns for 350,000 miners. Although the National Industrial Recovery Act was ultimately deemed unconstitutional by the Supreme Court in 1935 and replaced by the Wagner Act two months after that, it fueled workers to join unions and strengthened those organizations. ... The nature and power of organized labor in the United States is the outcome of historical tensions among counter-acting forces involving workplace rights, wages, working hours, political expression, labor laws, and other working conditions. Organized unions and their umbrella labor federations such as the AFL–CIO and citywide federations have competed, evolved, merged, and split against a backdrop of changing values and priorities, and periodic federal government intervention. The International Ladies’ Garment Workers’ Union (ILGWU) was one of the largest labor unions in the United States in the 1900s.
In 1909, 23-year-old Clara Lemlich galvanized a crowd of workers meeting at Cooper Union.[1] She climbed up to the speakers’ platform and declared: “I have no further patience for talk.

The ILGWU was an early example of an “industrial union.” In this setup, all workers in an industry would join the same union, regardless of their individual jobs or skill sets.
But the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire the following year showed that much more was needed.[2] One hundred and forty-six garment workers died in the conflagration.
As the union grew and diversified, the disconnect between its leadership and its membership could be contentious.
Women leaders like Rose Pesotta had long complained that the top leadership was almost exclusively male even though most members were women.

Pesotta, who had led the grueling Dressmakers General Strike in Los Angeles in 1933, resigned from the ILGWU’s General Executive Board in 1942.[3] Frustrated by the sexism she experienced from male leadership, she charged that the "men to whom I have been so useful" chose not to recognize her competence as a leader.
As the racial diversity of the union increased, members of color demanded that they be represented too.
Originally written as entertainment for strikers on picket lines, it starred a cast of garment workers and became a Broadway hit.

In the 1990s, the ILGWU merged with the Amalgamated Clothing and Textile Workers Union to form the new Union of Needletrades, Industrial and Textile Employees (UNITE), now UNITE HERE.

It represented hundreds of thousands of clothing industry workers, most of them women.
Two successful strikes in 1909 and 1910 won power for the union.
The strike became known as the “Uprising of 20,000.” At the time, it was the largest strike by women workers in US history.
The strikers demanded better hours, safer conditions, and fairer pay.
They received support from a group of wealthy women who organized via the Women’s Trade Union League (WTUL).
Supporters of industrial unionism argued that it would promote more unity and solidarity than the older style of “craft unionism,” which divided workers by their job function or skill level.
It galvanized leaders like Frances Perkins , who went on to shape the policies of the New Deal.
Expansion, Diversification, and Criticism Under the leadership of longtime president David Dubinsky (1932-1966), the ILGWU more than doubled its membership.
But local leaders like Sue Ko Lee in San Francisco and Emma Tenayuca in San Antonio worked with the ILGWU to win improvements for their communities.
It developed workers’ education programs that trained members not only in the ins and outs of organizing a strike, but also in history, economics, and international relations.

Later Years In the 1970s and 1980s, the garment industry in the US began to decline as companies competed with cheaper imports from overseas.
In response, the ILGWU mounted a campaign to encourage consumers to buy union-made American goods.

Brig. Gen. Saturday’s toll reflected the rapid worsening of Yemen’s civil war, where a yearslong truce fell apart over the summer. Fighting has escalated between the Iranian-backed Houthis — who control Sanaa, the north and the west of the country — and their Saudi-backed opponents based in the south and east. On Friday, an airstrike in a market in southern Yemen killed at least 30 people, according to Houthi officials. The Houthis and Yemen’s Saudi-backed military each blamed the other for that strike. Images show young children among the wounded Footage from Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV showed hospital staff carrying limp bodies of multiple young children from ambulances after Saturday’s strikes. Almost 30 people from the community based in northeastern Nagaland, a mountainous state bordering Myanmar, travelled to Britain for the ceremony, which the museum's director, Laura Van Broekhoven, called a "historic moment". The handover at the Pitt Rivers Museum came as part of a broader trend among Western museums reassessing how they acquired exhibits from other cultures, particularly human remains, and in some cases returning them. The Naga people once practiced headhunting, severing heads of enemies as trophies, but also kept heads of their own chiefs "at the centre of the villages" and one of the remains is a chief's head, said anthropologist Dolly Kikon, a member of Nagaland's Lotha-Naga community.

Almost 30 people from the community based in northeastern Nagaland, a mountainous state bordering Myanmar, travelled to Britain for the ceremony, which the museum's director, Laura Van Broekhoven, called a "historic moment".

The handover at the Pitt Rivers Museum came as part of a broader trend among Western museums reassessing how they acquired exhibits from other cultures, particularly human remains, and in some cases returning them.

Naga tribal leaders united for the handover and planned to bury the remains together under a joint memorial in a park.
